items.lbText:
Andy Burnham pledged a new lease of life for Britain’s high streets. We look at how he can achieve it

Save high street with higher online sales taxes, PM urged

Middleton’s revival could be blueprint for other towns

On the road to Downing Street, Andy Burnham promised a new dawn for Britain’s towns and high streets.

For too long places outside the big cities had been “forgotten or written off”, he argued after the Makerfield byelection. To help towns like those in his constituency, he said his government would make sure that the places Westminster had neglected would now get fairness.

Four times more people live in Britain’s towns than in cities. Since the turn of the millennium, big cities and more prosperous towns have grown significantly faster than weaker local economies. In Manchester, the population rose by almost a third , amid a renaissance in Cottonopolis that its former mayor capitalised on before entering No 10.

In sharp contrast, towns have been growing more slowly than cities on average, and are ageing faster as well. Some are in population decline, including Barrow-in-Furness in Cumbria (6%), Peterlee in County Durham (11%) and Rishton in Lancashire (13%).

To turn things around, experts say the prime minister will need to nurture the ingredients of local economic success. Here we chart five of the critical components.

Roughly every five years official estimates of local deprivation in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are made using a range of statistics for an index of multiple deprivation.

Each metric is critical for a town’s success: income, employment, education, health, crime, housing and the living environment.

Jaywick Sands , near Clacton-on-Sea in Essex, has led the rankings in England since 2010. The least deprived neighbourhood is in the town of Harpenden, near St Albans in Hertfordshire.

Most parts of the country have pockets of deprivation. But there are also clear patterns: towns, particularly in the north of England, the Midlands and in coastal areas , typically have the highest share of the most deprived neighbourhoods.

When it comes to the vitality of a town, income and employment levels are critical for supporting high streets. Boston in Lincolnshire has the lowest level of resident earnings in Great Britain, with people earnings about half as much as those in St Albans. Employment levels are lowest in Gravesham in Kent, followed by Blaenau Gwent in south Wales and Hyndburn in Lancashire.

After more than a decade of austerity, local authorities across the UK lack the financial firepower to meet rising demand for critical public services and to support economic activity.

The low point was reached in about 2019, when local spending power in England had been cut by about a quarter from 2010 levels. Analysis by the Institute for Government shows the most deprived local authorities ended up with significantly deeper cuts than affluent ones.

Funding levels have started to recover but will take until at least 2028-29 to return to 2010 levels after inflation is taken into account.

Transport and other physical infrastructure – including housing, superfast broadband, water and power – are central to the prosperity of a place. High standards of healthcare and education provision are also vital. Without these ingredients, households will struggle to reach their local high street or travel to work. Businesses will also lack access to a skilled, healthy workforce.

During the 2010s more than one in four bus services were cut in England . Rural communities and towns suffered most. Subsidies have been cut, and – as with trains – fares have risen. Burnham has made public control over buses and cheaper fares a priority. Official figures show Warrington, the prime minister’s home town , had the biggest fall in miles travelled by bus since 2010 of any English local authority.

Regions outside London and the south-east have also had significantly lower levels of investment .

Retail accounts for 5% of the UK economy and less than a 10th of employment. But its visible position on the high street gives it outsize influence on public perception about local economic performance.

Over the past two decades the internet has transformed the high street. Online spending has rocketed from less than 3% of total retail sales in Great Britain in 2006 to more than 25%. As a consequence, many mainstream shops have either closed or been replaced by vape shops, bookmakers and barbers. Official data shows high street retail employment has fallen most in the East Midlands.

Retailers have suffered from weaker levels of consumer demand amid the cost of living crisis – compounding the challenge in places where households are feeling the pinch most. Closures have been most pronounced in the north of England, the Midlands and deprived coastal towns.

Analysis by the Centre for Cities shows places where retailers pay higher rents (which it said could reflect resilient consumer demand) typically have the lowest vacancy rates. At one end of the scale is London, with high rents and 7% of shops with shutters drawn. At the other is Newport, where despite low costs, 19% of all units lie empty.

Social capital – the strength of communities, relationships and trust – is a key ingredient of economic success, not just a nice to have. However, Britain has suffered a hollowing out of the associations, clubs, organisations and infrastructure that were once the beating hearts of communities.

Local council spending on culture, sport and other related areas such as tourism and libraries has nosedived since 2010. Towns and rural areas have faced bigger cuts than big cities. Figures show councils spent a net £92.84 per person on culture in 2010-11 after adjusting for inflation. That has halved – last year a net £46.43 a head went on culture and sport.…

items.lbText:
Turnaround initiated by Andy Burnham and led by Steve Coogan could provide blueprint for other neglected areas

Save high street by taxing online sales at higher rate, Burnham urged

What makes a good town? Here are five key ingredients

T he former England footballer Paul Scholes and the actor Steve Coogan stare out from beside a fish and chip shop in Middleton, near Manchester . Looming over a mural of the pair – and the whole town – is an enormous former cotton mill that powered its economy a century ago.

The deafening looms and spindles of Warwick Mill fell silent decades ago, replaced in recent years by TikTok “urban explorers” who share videos of themselves crawling through its abandoned shell.

Yet the old building may have life inside it yet: last month Rochdale council wrestled Warwick Mill out of the hands of its absentee owner, a millionaire Chinese businessman, under whom it had been derelict for years.

Now the Grade II-listed site is at the centre of plans Andy Burnham believes could turn Middleton, where he was once a trainee journalist , into a blueprint for the future of Britain’s struggling towns.

“It used to be good,” said Dorothy Kersh, in the town square with her husband, Ernie, both of them 83. “In the 70s we had a cinema, we had banks. It’s lost character and we’ve hardly got any shops. We haven’t even got a bank now – I never thought NatWest would leave Middleton. It’s just going downhill.”

Middleton, a town of about 50,000 people a few miles from both Manchester and Rochdale, is in the type of existential crisis suffered by most British towns.

A decade or so ago, locals could find virtually everything they needed in its neat square of grocers, butchers and banks. But a giant Tesco has hoovered up the cash since it opened in 2013, compounding the rise of online and out-of-town shopping.

In addition to the loss of all its banks, the town saw the remains of its last post office closed by Modella Capital, the new private equity owner of WH Smith , days before Burnham became prime minister.

Now the shopping precinct offers little more than bookmakers, vape shops, pawnbrokers and fast-food outlets.

Its geographical identity feels muddled. Middleton was historically in Lancashire but has a Manchester postcode and dialling code, although residents pay their council tax to Rochdale. The region’s lauded tram network does not stop here.

“It’s really a dying town,” said Tim King, outside a large post office branch that closed down years ago. “We’ve only got one cash machine and that’s at Tesco, and there’s never any money in it. We’ve lost out on the trams. We haven’t got anything down here, to be honest.”

But six miles from the birthplace of the modern co-operative movement in 1844, a community fightback is under way.

Months before he departed for Downing Street, Burnham launched a mayoral development corporation for Middleton, giving local leaders power to set lower business rates, acquire underused land and property, and build 1,500 new homes.

The body is led by Coogan, the Bafta-winning creator of Alan Partridge, and Rose Marley, the chief executive of Co-operatives UK. Crucially, residents and business owners will have a seat at the table: a survey of 2,000 Middletonians is shaping the agenda of this new mayoral body – with Warwick Mill and other empty buildings identified by locals as an immediate priority.

Wearing a hard hat and hi-vis vest during a tour of Warwick Mill last month, Coogan said the Middleton of his childhood was a “thriving” town but that “over the last 35 years there has been a kind of a bank ride” by firms registered in the British Virgin Islands, China and the US: “All that money has been extracted but very little has been put back into the infrastructure.”

Coogan said the project was about more than attempting to revitalise his home town. It was a chance to reverse the political and economic malaise that has seen former Labour voters shift to rightwing populist parties such as Reform UK in post-industrial areas across Britain.

“There’s a problem in this country which is post-industrial neglect,” he told the Guardian. “The idea, the Blairite approach: it’s called multinationalism, there is nothing we can do, throw your hands up, you’ve just got to see what happens, we can’t help these people .

“Leaving that vacuum will mean that the extremists, populist extremists, will fill that gap. That’s the problem with top-down, well-meaning, but disempowering, philanthropic, centralised socialism . People don’t want to receive charity, they want to be empowered .”

Coogan is part of a group called Middleton Co-operating, which aims to “rewire the whole of the economy locally” by taking infrastructure and everyday essentials into public control.

Its plans include using renewable energy, such as solar panels and small wind turbines, to help power a secondary school and a hospice. A trial involving heat pumps and solar panels on a terrace of Edwardian homes is also being put together.

Banks could soon return too, with plans for a banking hub where Lloyds, NatWest and others could open on different days of the week, alongside financial advisers.

The group, which was backed by Burnham when he was mayor and in June won £4.5m funding from the national lottery’s solidarity fund, wants to expand into food production, early years support, mental health provision and adult social care.

“These are all things that have the biggest impact on people’s day-to-day lives and they’re generally all owned by big business and private equity – they cost too much and are a cause of a lot of stress in the community,” said Mark Fraser, a founder of Middleton Co-operating.…

See if you can do a better job than John Healey at creating a budget that keeps MPs and the bond markets onside

On 28 October, John Healey will announce the autumn budget to parliament. As in all years, the chancellor has to strike a balance between the following:

Raising the money needed to fund the services that voters demand.

Keeping taxes at levels that are acceptable to voters.

Persuading the government’s creditors in the bond markets that it will continue to be able to pay its debts.

In our game you get to try your hand at designing a successful budget. Can you keep backbenchers happy without upsetting the bond markets? And can you do it all while keeping the books balanced? Just like the real chancellor, you begin in the red.

At the spring statement, Healey’s immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had left herself £23.6bn of “headroom” against the fiscal rules, which require day-to-day spending to be matched by receipts by the end of this parliament. However, the buffer is widely expected to have been slashed by a surge in debt interest costs, as the war in the Middle East triggers a global inflation shock that is rattling the bond markets.

Taken together, the Resolution Foundation thinktank predicts the headroom against the government’s fiscal target will be halved, to about £12bn.

Healey is thought to be willing to allow the buffer to take a hit. However, jittery bond investors are looking for him to retain a degree of headroom to guard against further negative shocks, with at least £14bn thought to be needed to avoid provoking a bond market reaction.

The chancellor is also under pressure to find space in the public finances for three things: a cost of living support package; a boost in defence spending; and financing Andy Burnham’s long-term priority to spread “good growth” to every postcode.

Solving the above is all part of your task. You’ll see the headroom grow or shrink, or – most worrying – become negative in response to your policy decision. But keep an eye on the alerts on how the markets – which may not be convinced – and the opinion polls are responding as you go. Good luck.

If you get stuck tap or click for Treasury briefings – chart icon – and wry notes from Burnham – note icon – for guidance.

Sources and notes: the estimates of income from each of the measures and for the current government balance come from a variety of economists and thinktanks and the government’s own assumptions. The core fiscal impacts are from HM Revenue and Customs, and the estimates for other measures are sourced in the descriptions. These estimates are often based on those economists’ own assumptions about future growth, inflation, collection rates and other variables. So this game should be seen as illustrative of the relative sizes of the impacts of measures. Do not buy or sell gilts on the basis of this game, in case you were thinking of it.

items.lbText:
Dr Alex Chapman calls for a government-funded price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas, in response to an article by Nils Pratley

Nils Pratley thinks that the secretary of state, Miatta Fahnbulleh, should “keep things simple” and develop a targeted social tariff to protect vulnerable households from surging energy bills ( The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff, 14 October ). Unfortunately, there is nothing simple about such a scheme.

Pratley’s proposal would mean creating a new benefits system inside our privatised energy industry. If the interminable debates about our current benefits system were not enough to put him off, we can look to the failing social care system to see where it might lead. Andy Burnham has made it his life’s mission to dismantle this lottery that can strip pensioners of their savings and the family home. Just as he now plans a universal public provision of adult social care, we at the New Economics Foundation have such a plan for energy.

Every household should be able to afford the energy essentials: enough warmth to survive a winter; enough electricity to switch on the lights and run a fridge. We should recognise this as a universal right rather than waste time tinkering with a targeting system that arbitrarily separates the “worthy” from the “unworthy” (the “rough justice” of the Resolution Foundation’s proposal , which penalises households based on the income of the highest earner, is a case in point).

The long-term design of a universal offer can be debated. But as another energy crisis bears down on us, we should keep it simple: have the Treasury fund a true price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas. This would be a policy from which everyone wins (especially if electrically heated homes are allowed to transfer across their gas allowance).

In the longer term, one way to help pay for this could be to charge households with very high energy consumption more. But there are other ways. The Australian “ solar sharer ” scheme gives every household three hours of free electricity in the middle of the day, bringing hope that renewables could soon give true energy security. Dr Alex Chapman Head of economic and environmental policy, New Economics Foundation
